--- title: "The raw recording" --- This page opens one EEG recording and looks at what is in it, before anything has been cleaned. By the end you should be able to say: - what a recording file contains, - where each electrode sits on the head, - how the recording knows when each stimulus appeared, and - how to check that the recording and the task's own trial list agree. You do not need to write code. Run each cell, read what comes out, and try the changes suggested under **Try it**. ## The recording The participant sat in front of a screen wearing a cap of 64 electrodes. On each trial a striped disc appeared; they pressed one of two keys to say whether it was an "A" or a "B", and were told whether they were right. The file below holds the first 100 trials of their first visit, about six minutes. ::: {#40466b8c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from pathlib import Path import mne data = Path("data/eeg_tutorial_data_v1") raw = mne.io.read_raw_fif(data / "sub-01/raw/sub-01_visit-1_task_raw.fif", preload=True) print(raw.info["sfreq"], "samples per second") print(len(raw.ch_names), "channels") print(round(raw.times[-1]), "seconds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 512.0 samples per second 67 channels 376 seconds ``` ::: ::: The first lines say where the data are and load a library called MNE-Python [@gramfort2013], the free toolbox for EEG analysis that the whole tutorial uses. Everything you learn to do with it here you can do with your own data later. An EEG recording is a table of numbers. Each **channel** is one row: the voltage at one electrode, measured again and again. The **sampling rate** says how often: 512 times a second here. So six minutes of 67 channels is about 12 million numbers. The channels are not all scalp electrodes: ::: {#eed39115 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(raw.ch_names) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['A1', 'A2', 'A3', 'A4', 'A5', 'A6', 'A7', 'A8', 'A9', 'A10', 'A11', 'A12', 'A13', 'A14', 'A15', 'A16', 'A17', 'A18', 'A19', 'A20', 'A21', 'A22', 'A23', 'A24', 'A25', 'A26', 'A27', 'A28', 'A29', 'A30', 'A31', 'A32', 'B1', 'B2', 'B3', 'B4', 'B5', 'B6', 'B7', 'B8', 'B9', 'B10', 'B11', 'B12', 'B13', 'B14', 'B15', 'B16', 'B17', 'B18', 'B19', 'B20', 'B21', 'B22', 'B23', 'B24', 'B25', 'B26', 'B27', 'B28', 'B29', 'B30', 'B31', 'B32', 'EXG1', 'EXG2', 'Status'] ``` ::: ::: - `A1` to `A32` and `B1` to `B32` are the 64 scalp electrodes. The names are the sockets on the amplifier, not places on the head. We fix that below. - `EXG1` and `EXG2` are two extra electrodes stuck on the face, beside and below the left eye. They pick up eye movements and blinks, which we will need in the next chapter. - `Status` is not a voltage from the body at all. It is the **trigger channel**, explained further down. ## Looking at the signal Always look at the raw signal before doing anything else. Here are ten seconds from ten electrodes. ::: {#c1c210a5 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw.plot(start=100, duration=10, picks=["A1", "A5", "A13", "A21", "A28", "B1", "B5", "B13", "B21", "B28"], scalings=dict(eeg=40e-6), show_scrollbars=False); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](02-raw-data_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=717 height=761} ::: ::: Each trace is one electrode; time runs left to right. Two things to notice. **The signals are tiny.** The scale bar is 80 microvolts (millionths of a volt). Brain signals at the scalp are a few tens of microvolts at most [@luck2014], far smaller than the heartbeat signal on an ECG. **Much of what you see is not brain activity.** The fast fuzz on every trace is mostly interference from the building's mains wiring. The large bumps between 102 and 104 seconds, biggest on `A1` and `B1`, are blinks: those two electrodes sit on the forehead, just above the eyes. Chapter 3 is about removing both. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Change `start=100` to another time (anything from 0 to 350) and run the cell again. Find a moment where one big deflection appears on several channels at once. ::: ## Where the electrodes are The cap follows a standard layout. Telling the software which layout gives each channel a proper name and a position on the head. ::: {#da413544 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} layout = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("biosemi64") raw.rename_channels(dict(zip(raw.ch_names[:64], layout.ch_names))) raw.set_montage(layout) raw.plot_sensors(show_names=True); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](02-raw-data_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=779 height=766} ::: ::: This is the head seen from above, nose at the top. The names follow a standard scheme [@oostenveld2001] with a rule worth learning: - The letter is the region: **F** frontal, **C** central, **P** parietal, **O** occipital (the back of the head, over visual cortex), **T** temporal (above the ears). - **Odd numbers are on the left, even numbers on the right**, and **z** ("zero") is the midline. So `Oz` is at the back in the middle, and `F3` is at the front on the left. Our stimulus is visual, so expect the earliest brain responses around `Oz`, `O1` and `O2`. ## Triggers: how the recording knows what happened when The EEG amplifier knows nothing about the task. To link the two, the task computer sends a short pulse down a cable every time something happens, and the amplifier records it alongside the brain signals in the `Status` channel. The size of the pulse is a code for what happened. These pulses are called **triggers** (or event markers). ::: {#e5cb6034 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} events = mne.find_events(raw, stim_channel="Status") print(len(events), "triggers") print(events[:8]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 400 triggers [[2853 0 11] [3542 0 20] [4011 0 31] [4190 0 41] [4719 0 11] [5385 0 28] [5777 0 30] [5956 0 41]] ``` ::: ::: Each row is one trigger. The first number is *when* (counted in samples from the start of the file), and the last is the *code*. Ignore the middle one. For this task the codes mean: ::: {#6f331097 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} codes = {"trial start": 11, "stimulus A": 20, "stimulus B": 28, "response A": 30, "response B": 31, "feedback correct": 40, "feedback wrong": 41} ``` ::: Here are the first 20 seconds of triggers, one row per kind of event. ::: {#cae577ab .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} first = events[events[:, 0] < 20 * raw.info["sfreq"]] mne.viz.plot_events(first, sfreq=raw.info["sfreq"], event_id=codes, on_missing="ignore"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](02-raw-data_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=653 height=393} ::: ::: Read it from left to right and you can see the task: a trial starts, a stimulus appears, the participant responds, feedback follows, and it all repeats about every three and a half seconds. ::: {.callout-note} ## Why this matters Everything later in the tutorial depends on triggers. To see the brain's response to a stimulus we cut out the signal around each stimulus trigger and average those pieces. If the triggers are wrong, every result after them is wrong, and nothing will warn you. ::: ## Check the recording against the task's own records The task program also saved a table with one row per trial. ::: {#6f1ac3ed .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd trials = pd.read_csv(data / "sub-01/raw/sub-01_visit-1_task_behaviour.csv") trials.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
trial phase cat x y resp fb rt
0 0 train A 51.2219 67.9577 B Incorrect 913.4243
1 1 train B 53.2355 22.3234 A Incorrect 753.5773
2 2 train A 61.9324 74.0866 B Incorrect 902.2831
3 3 train B 68.8337 54.1048 A Incorrect 1523.7676
4 4 train B 82.9823 64.7882 B Correct 1687.6825
``` ::: ::: `cat` is the stimulus's true category, `resp` is what the participant answered, `fb` the feedback they saw and `rt` the reaction time in milliseconds. (`x` and `y` describe the stimulus: how wide its stripes were and how tilted.) We now have two independent records of the same session. They should agree. First check: is there one stimulus trigger per trial, and does its code match the trial's category? ::: {#1a4dc0a8 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} stimuli = events[(events[:, 2] == 20) | (events[:, 2] == 28)] trials["trigger"] = stimuli[:, 2] pd.crosstab(trials["cat"], trials["trigger"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
trigger 20 28
cat
A 52 0
B 0 48
``` ::: ::: Every category-A trial has code 20 and every category-B trial has code 28, with nothing in the other corners. Good. Second check: the triggers give us our own measure of reaction time, the gap between the stimulus trigger and the response trigger. Does it match the `rt` the task program wrote down? ::: {#cd96d4f0 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} responses = events[(events[:, 2] == 30) | (events[:, 2] == 31)] gap_ms = (responses[:, 0] - stimuli[:, 0]) / raw.info["sfreq"] * 1000 (gap_ms - trials["rt"]).describe().round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` count 100.0 mean 9.2 std 4.9 min 0.1 25% 5.5 50% 8.3 75% 13.3 max 18.6 Name: rt, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: The two agree to within 20 milliseconds on every trial. The trigger gap is a little longer, by 9 ms on average; that small delay comes from the screen and the cable, and is normal. What would *not* be normal is a difference of hundreds of milliseconds, or one that grows over the session. That would mean the two records are out of step. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Try it Use the triggers to work out how many of these 100 trials the participant got right: count the triggers with code 40. Then check your answer against the table with `(trials["fb"] == "Correct").sum()`. ::: ## What is wrong with this recording Nothing unusual, but it is not ready to analyse. One plot shows two of the problems. It splits the signal by **frequency**: how much of it is slow waves, and how much is fast. ::: {#e4fd2340 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} raw.compute_psd(fmax=120, picks="eeg").plot(average=True); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](02-raw-data_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=971 height=347} ::: ::: - The sharp spike at **50 Hz** is the mains electricity (Australian power lines alternate 50 times a second). It is the fuzz you saw on the traces. - The steep rise at the far left is very slow **drift**: the voltage at each electrode wandering over seconds as the skin and gel settle. Neither comes from the brain. The next chapter removes them, along with blinks, and turns this continuous recording into clean trials. One feature of this plot *is* brain activity: the bump at about 11 Hz. That is the **alpha rhythm**, the most prominent rhythm in the human EEG and the first to be described [@berger1929]. It gets its own chapter later. ## Summary - A recording is channels by samples. Most channels are scalp electrodes; some are helpers (eye electrodes, the trigger channel). - Electrode names tell you where they are: letter for region, odd for left, even for right, z for the midline. - Triggers tie the brain recording to the task. Always check them against the task's own trial table before going further. - Raw EEG is mostly not brain signal. Cleaning comes next. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## In the lab's real pipeline The full recordings are 40 minutes at 4096 samples per second, about 2 GB per visit. The trigger check on this page is done for every recording by an audit script before any preprocessing is allowed to run, and a recording that fails it is not used. :::
